claims: A filibuster is a U.S. Senate tactic used to prolong debate and delay or block a vote on legislation.
A filibuster effectively requires a 60-vote supermajority to invoke cloture and end debate.
The filibuster originated from an 1806 rule change.
The filibuster allows a minority to obstruct majority action.
The longest individual filibuster speech lasted 25 hours and 5 minutes by Sen. Cory Booker in April 2025.
To overcome a filibuster, the Senate must pass a cloture motion.
A cloture motion currently requires 60 votes (three-fifths of the Senate) to limit further debate and move to a final vote, explains the Brennan Center for Justice.
Modern filibusters rarely require senators to hold the floor with speeches, according to PBS Newshour.
Modern filibusters allow blocking legislation by merely threatening a filibuster, according to PBS Newshour.
The filibuster has been removed for Supreme Court nominations and most other judicial/federal appointments, according to this YouTube video.
The filibuster was an unintended consequence of removing a rule in 1806 that allowed for a simple majority to end debate, notes this YouTube video.
The Senate adopted the cloture rule in 1917 to enable a two-thirds majority to end a filibuster, according to the U.S. Senate.
Throughout the mid-20th century, the filibuster was heavily used by Southern senators to block civil rights legislation, notes the Center for American Progress.
Sen. Strom Thurmond held the floor for 24 hours and 18 minutes against the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
Sen. Cory Booker recorded 25 hours and 5 minutes against the policies of the Trump administration in April 2025.
The traditional "talking filibuster" was made famous by Mr. Smith Goes to Washington.
